t: IDEs, translators, data types, variables and operators
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP19: IDEs, translators, data types, variables and operators.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Describe how the tools in an IDE help a programmer write, translate and debug code. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Once an algorithm has been designed, a programmer expresses it in a programming language such as C sharp. The result is source code: text that people can read and edit but that the processor cannot execute directly. Programmers usually work inside an integrated development environment (IDE), which combines an editor, a translator and debugging tools in one application so that code can be written, checked, run and corrected quickly. Before the program can run, its source code must be translated into machine code, the binary instructions the processor understands; this job is done by an assembler, a compiler or an interpreter, each working in a different way. Inside the program, data is held in variables.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Each variable has an identifier and a data type, which decides what values it can hold, how much memory is reserved and which operations make sense. Values that must never change are declared as constants. Operators then do the work: arithmetic operators calculate, relational operators compare values to give true or false, and Boolean operators combine those conditions. Finally, programs communicate with users through input and output, converting text typed at the keyboard into numbers and formatting results neatly on screen. These ideas are the foundation for every program you will write in the AS course.
Right. What else do we need to know?

An IDE is a software application that gives programmers a complete set of tools for developing software. Its editor lets code be written, edited and saved, and most editors are smart: syntax highlighting colours keywords, strings and comments differently, automatic indentation shows which statements belong inside which blocks, and line numbers and code folding make long programs easier to navigate. A syntax checker underlines invalid code as it is typed, and code completion (called IntelliSense in Visual Studio) suggests keywords and identifiers after a few letters, improving speed and reducing spelling errors. Preferences allow a team to agree layout rules, such as whether an opening brace goes on its own line, and the IDE can apply them automatically so everyone's code looks the same when it is combined.
Got it. Keep going.

The IDE also contains or connects to a compiler, so the program can be built and run with a single command, and any translation errors are listed with their line numbers. Finally, debugging tools allow the programmer to set breakpoints, step through code one line at a time and watch the values of variables, which makes locating errors far easier. Debugging techniques are covered in more detail in AP23.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Translation is the conversion of a program from the language it was written in into machine code that the processor can execute. An assembler translates assembly language, a low-level language in which each mnemonic, such as LDA or ADD, corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction. High-level languages are translated by compilers or interpreters. A compiler translates the whole program before any of it runs. If errors are found, it produces an error report and no executable is created until every error is corrected, after which the program must be compiled again. Because the compiler sees the complete program, it can optimise the object code, so the finished program runs quickly and can be distributed without its source code.
Okay. Keep going.

An interpreter translates one statement, executes it, then moves to the next. It produces no object code, so the source code and interpreter are needed every time the program runs, and execution is slower. Errors are only discovered when the faulty line is reached, which may be after earlier statements have already changed files or data. However, interpreters give immediate feedback, which makes them useful during development and debugging. C sharp combines both ideas: source code is compiled to an intermediate language, which the dot NET runtime compiles to machine code just in time.
Go on.

A variable is a named location in memory that stores a single value which can change while the program is running. Its name is called its identifier. Most languages, including C sharp, require variables to be declared before use: the declaration states the data type and identifier so that the right amount of memory can be reserved, and it may also give an initial value. Assignment, using a single equals sign, replaces the current value with a new one.
Right. Keep going.

Identifiers must follow the language's rules: in C sharp they begin with a letter or underscore, contain only letters, digits and underscores, cannot contain spaces, cannot be reserved keywords and are case-sensitive, so total and Total are different variables. Conventions are not enforced by the compiler but should be followed so that code is readable: use meaningful names such as ticketPrice rather than tp, and write variables in camelCase. A constant is a named value fixed when the program is written, declared in C sharp with const. Using a constant for a value such as a VAT rate or a maximum group size means it cannot be changed accidentally while the program runs, its purpose is clear from its name, and if it ever needs updating it is changed in one place only.
Go on.

A data type defines what kind of value a variable can hold, how much memory it needs and which operations can be performed on it. C sharp uses int for whole numbers such as counts and ages, and double for real numbers such as measurements and averages. For money, decimal is better than double because it stores decimal fractions exactly, avoiding small binary rounding errors. A char holds exactly one character in single quotes, a string holds any sequence of characters in double quotes, and a bool holds only true or false. The choice should match how the data will be used, not just what it looks like.
Makes sense. Keep going.

A telephone number or a membership code made of digits should be a string, because it may start with a zero, may contain spaces and will never be used in arithmetic. A yes/no fact, such as whether a fee has been paid, should be Boolean because there are only two possible states. Choosing the right type saves memory, prevents meaningless operations and lets the compiler detect mistakes, such as trying to store text in an integer. Converting between types is called casting: (int)7.9 truncates to 7, while (double)total forces real rather than integer division.
Go on.

Arithmetic operators in C sharp are +, -, *, or and %. When both operands of or are integers, C sharp performs integer division and discards the remainder, so 17 or 5 gives 3; if either operand is real, the result is real, so 17.0 or 5 gives 3.4. The modulus operator % gives the remainder, so 17 % 5 gives 2. Together, div and mod split a quantity into whole units and what is left, for example converting minutes into hours and minutes, and n % 2 equals 0 tests whether a number is even. Shorthand operators include ++ to add one and += to add a value to a variable.
Got it. Keep going.

Relational operators ( equals, not equal to, <, less than or equal to, >, greater than or equal to ) compare two values and always produce a Boolean result. Boolean operators combine conditions: and (AND) is true only when both sides are true, or (OR) is true when either or both are true, and ! (NOT) reverses a value. To evaluate a condition by hand, substitute the values, work out any brackets first, replace each comparison with true or false, then apply the Boolean operators. Brackets make the intended order clear, since and is evaluated before or. Watch for the classic slip of writing equals (assignment) when equals (comparison) is meant.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Data type?
A classification of data that determines the values a variable can hold, the memory it needs and the operations that can be performed on it.
Variable?
A named location in memory that stores a single value which can change while the program runs.
Constant?
A named value that is set when the program is written and cannot change while the program runs.
Identifier?
The name given to a variable, constant or subroutine so that it can be referred to in a program.
Syntax?
The set of rules that define how valid statements must be written in a programming language.
Integrated development environment (IDE)?
A software application that provides the tools needed to develop programs, such as an editor, translator and debugging tools, in one place.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions on this lesson use the command words state, describe and explain. To describe IDE features, name the feature and say how it helps, for example 'syntax highlighting colours keywords so the structure is easier to read' rather than just listing tools; three features are typically worth one or two marks each. For translators, mark schemes credit clear contrasts: a compiler translates the whole program before execution and produces an executable, while an interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time and produces no object code; an assembler translates assembly language with a one-to-one mapping. Avoid saying an interpreter 'has no errors' or that a compiler 'runs the program line by line'. When asked to define a variable, include that it is a named memory location whose value can change during execution. For data type questions, give the type and, when asked, a reason tied to how the data is used: phone numbers are strings because of the leading zero and no arithmetic. When evaluating expressions, show the substituted values, take care with integer division and mod, and give Boolean results as true or false. Common mistakes are using a real type for a count, and confusing equals with equals.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A program stores a customer's mobile number, such as 07700 900123. Which data type is most suitable? Is it A, int; B, double; C, string; D, bool?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: string. It has a leading zero and a space and is never used in calculations, so a string keeps it exactly as entered.
